claims.text: Stripe's minions produce over 1,300 pull requests merged each week that are completely minion-produced and human-reviewed, containing no human-written code, up from 1,000 as of Part 1.
Stripe Minions authored roughly 7,000 merged PRs in one week (about 30% of all Stripe PRs) as of August 2026, up from 1,300+ in February 2026.
Over a thousand pull requests merged each week at Stripe were completely minion-produced as of the Part 1 post dated 2026-02-09.
A typical minion run starts in a Slack message and ends in a pull request that passes CI and is ready for human review, with no interaction in between.
A Stripe devbox is an AWS EC2 instance that contains Stripe's source code and runs services under development; devboxes are 'cattle, not pets', i.e. standardized and easy to replace.

Stripe aims for a devbox to be ready within 10 seconds by proactively provisioning and warming a pool of devboxes, including cloning large git repositories, warming Bazel and type-checking caches, and starting code generation services.
After the 10-second spin-up, a devbox is checked out to a recent copy of master across all of Stripe's main repos.
Devboxes were built for human engineers long before LLM coding agents existed; a Stripe engineer might have half a dozen running at a time.
Devboxes are isolated from production resources and the internet, so minions can run on them without human permission checks.
Because the quarantined devbox confines mistakes to the blast radius of one devbox, the minion agent runs with full permissions and skips confirmation prompts.
Minion devboxes run in Stripe's QA environment, so minions have no access to real user data, Stripe's production services, or arbitrary network egress.
Stripe also has an internal security control framework that prevents minions from using their MCP tools to perform destructive actions.
Devbox-based parallelization avoids the overhead of git worktrees, which Stripe says would not scale at Stripe.
Stripe's minion agent harness is an internal fork of Block's open-source goose made in late 2024, with development later focused on unattended minion needs rather than human-supervised use.
Blueprints are workflows defined in code that direct a minion run; each node can run either deterministic code or an agent loop focused on a task.

Agentic blueprint nodes include 'Implement task' and 'Fix CI failures', which are given wide latitude, while deterministic nodes such as 'Run configured linters' and 'Push changes' invoke no LLM at all.
The minion blueprint resembles a state machine intermixing deterministic code nodes and free-flowing agent nodes.
Stripe says deterministically coding anticipated small decisions, such as always linting at the end of a run, saves tokens and CI costs at scale and gives the agent less opportunity to err.
Individual teams can build custom blueprints, for example to run LLM-assisted migrations that a fully deterministic codemod could not handle.
A subset of linters runs as a deterministic node in the blueprint, looped locally before the agent's branch is pushed so the branch has a fair chance of passing CI the first time.
Stripe's local lint executable uses heuristics to select and run lints on each git push, taking less than five seconds.
Stripe's test battery contains over three million tests, which CI runs selectively on a push.
After a minion pushes, CI runs and auto-applies autofixes for failing tests; failures without an autofix go back to a blueprint agent node for one more local fix attempt.

After the second push and CI run, the branch is sent back to its human operator for manual scrutiny; Stripe caps CI at at most two rounds because CI costs tokens, compute and time, with diminishing returns beyond that.

Once a minion finishes, it creates a branch, pushes it to CI, and prepares a pull request following Stripe's PR template; the engineer opens the PR and requests review from another Stripe engineer, or gives the minion further instructions.
